newsitem.title: USA: Ford confident Louisville plant met U.S. labor law.
newsitem.headline: Ford confident Louisville plant met U.S. labor law.

text.p: Ford Motor Co said Wednesday it was confident that hiring practices at its Louisville, Kentucky, assembly plant exceeded its obligations under labor law.
"Quite frankly we are surprised at the charges," said Ford spokeswoman Francine Romine-MacBride by telephone.
Earlier Wednesday, the U.S. Labor Department said it had filed a complaint against Ford alleging discrimination against women who applied for jobs at the Louisville plant in 1993.

The complaint said Ford discriminated against female applicants in its hiring and selection procedures for entry-level laborer positions at the plant. It also said Ford failed to cooperate with a probe by the Office of Federal Contract Compliance Programs (OFCCP) when the company denied investigators access to information they thought was relevant to the case, the Labor Department said.

"We believe the facts will demonstrate that the company cooperated fully with the OFCCP in its review and that the company's hiring practices more than complied with its obligations," said Romine-MacBride.

"Ford carefully designed this special program to ensure the company would interview and hire a greater percentage of women than were represented in comparable jobs in the local labor market. This effort was successful."
Ford said the percentage of women hired exceeded the representation of women in comparable jobs by more than 10 percent.
"Furthermore, Ford has not received a single complaint from any of the women interviewed, nor are we aware of any complaints having been filed elsewhere," the spokeswoman said.

The OFCCP enforces laws that prohibit job discrimination among federal contractors. Ford's Louisville assembly plant, which makes trucks, is considered a federal contractor since it sells some of the trucks it makes to the U.S. government.
